paragraphs.heading: A common carbonate
paragraphs.text: Calcite is a carbonate mineral made of calcium carbonate (CaCO₃). Calcium carbonate has more than one polymorph, and calcite is the most stable of them. The others are the minerals aragonite and vaterite. At temperatures above 300 °C, aragonite turns into calcite within days or less, and vaterite is less stable still. Calcite is a very common mineral, above all as a component of limestone.

paragraphs.heading: A name from lime
paragraphs.text: The word calcite comes from the German Calcit, a 19th-century term. That term goes back to calx, the Latin word for lime, joined to -ite, the suffix used for naming minerals. In geology and mineralogy, the term alabaster is reserved for a variety of gypsum. Archaeologists and people in the stone trade also use it for a similar-looking, translucent kind of calcite deposit that is fine-grained and banded.

paragraphs.heading: How to recognize it
paragraphs.text: Calcite is the mineral that defines hardness 3 on the Mohs scale, a scale of mineral hardness based on comparing scratch hardness. Its other diagnostic properties include a specific gravity of 2.71. Crystalline varieties also have a vitreous luster. It is white or has no color. When it is charged with impurities it can show shades of gray, brown, red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet or even black. Treating a sample with acid gives a characteristic fizzing, produced by carbon dioxide being released.

paragraphs.heading: A mineral of many shapes
paragraphs.text: Calcite takes numerous habits, which represent combinations of more than 1000 crystallographic forms. Among them are rhombohedra, tabular habits, prisms and various scalenohedra. It can also occur as fibrous, granular, lamellar or compact material. Some shapes have nicknames. Acute scalenohedral crystals are sometimes called "dogtooth spar", and the rhombohedral form is sometimes called "nailhead spar".

paragraphs.heading: Seeing double
paragraphs.text: Single crystals of calcite have an optical property called birefringence, or double refraction. This strong birefringence makes an object looked at through a clear piece of calcite appear doubled. The Danish scientist Rasmus Bartholin gave the first description of the effect, using calcite, in 1669. A transparent variety known as "Iceland spar" is used for optical purposes, and large calcite crystals go into optical equipment. The rhombohedral form may also have been the "sunstone" that the Icelandic Sagas say Viking navigators used.

paragraphs.heading: Light from impurities
paragraphs.text: Calcite ranges from transparent to opaque, and now and then it shows phosphorescence or fluorescence. It also has thermoluminescent properties, mainly because of impurities of divalent manganese (Mn²⁺). In one experiment, ions of several metals were added to calcite samples to see whether they gave off heat or light. When manganese and lead ions were both present, a reaction took place. Lead (Pb²⁺) and manganese (Mn²⁺) both worked as activators within the calcite lattice, though the lead was far less efficient than the manganese.
